About Me

CAPM-certified Project Coordinator with a track record of keeping complex projects on time, cross-functional teams aligned, and stakeholders informed. I care about the work behind the work — the communication, the planning, and the follow-through that most people don't see.

What I'm Looking For

I'm drawn to teams where projects are complex, communication matters, and no two days look the same. Ideally a company where I can grow into a senior PM role and contribute from day one — not just coordinate meetings, but help shape how work gets done.

My Outlook on AI
Featured 3 min read · Updated May 2026

After running an AI workshop at GCU, I noticed students often see AI as a shortcut, while teachers see it as a threat. Both miss the point. My view is that AI is only as powerful as the person using it. We need people who are willing to learn and use it. Those who don’t will fall behind because the world doesn’t slow down. What stood out most was seeing students be curious about it—that curiosity is what actually makes AI useful. The real question isn’t whether we should use AI, but what we’re trying to solve with it. Used well, it helps you think faster, explore ideas, and get unstuck. Used poorly, it replaces thinking. In project management, I see it the same way: it’s not about replacing work, but focusing on what actually matters.

The real question isn't "should we use AI?" — it's "what problems are we actually solving?" When students used AI to skip the thinking, they learned nothing. When they used it to explore ideas faster, test hypotheses, or get unstuck, it accelerated their learning.

In project management, AI works the same way. It's not about automating your job — it's about eliminating the noise so you can focus on what actually matters: understanding stakeholder needs, spotting risks before they become problems, and making decisions with incomplete information.

I use AI daily, but I treat it like any other tool in my PM toolkit: powerful when applied to the right problem, useless when you don't understand what you're trying to accomplish in the first place.
